sentences.text: The skull of Telmatosaurus measured approximately 40 centimeters in length and featured a narrow shape that rose significantly in height toward the rear.
Its teeth were tall and slender, with each tooth being only about four millimeters wide.
This dinosaur reached a length of roughly 5 meters and a mass of 600 kilograms, a size scientists attribute to insular dwarfism.
A juvenile specimen possesses a large, non-cancerous growth known as an ameloblastoma, a condition previously found only in modern mammals and reptiles.
Farmers uncovered a Telmatosaurus skull in 1895 at the Săcele estate within Transylvania and handed it over to Ilona Nopcsa.
Franz Nopcsa initially assigned the species the name Limnosaurus transsylvanicus in 1899.
He later renamed the genus Telmatosaurus in 1903 after realizing Limnosaurus was already occupied by a crocodilian described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1872.
Nopcsa also discovered that the name Limnosaurus had been used for a crocodile by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1872, prompting the 1903 renaming.
The generic name comes from the Greek word for 'swamp', indicating a belief that the animal lived in water.
In 1915, Nopcsa moved the species to the genus Orthomerus, calling it Orthomerus transsylvanicus.
Barnum Brown created the genus Hecatasaurus in 1910 without knowing about the name change, resulting in a later synonym.
Telmatosaurus consumed C3 plants, shrubs, herbaceous vegetation, leaves, and seeds.
The existence of an ameloblastoma in a dinosaur implies that the development of benign tumors is a fundamental trait.
Because only the lower jaws are preserved, the cause of death for the juvenile Telmatosaurus with the tumor remains unknown.
Since the preserved remains consist solely of the two lower jaws, no one can determine the cause of its death.
Telmatosaurus belongs to the class Ornithischia.
Magyar and colleagues named the clade containing Telmatosaurus, Kryptohadros, and Tethyshadros as Telmatosauridae.
The parent group of Telmatosaurus is Telmatosauridae.
The family of Telmatosaurus is Telmatosauridae.
The family classification of Telmatosaurus is listed as Hadrosauridae with uncertainty.
Current cladistic analyses suggest Telmatosaurus is either a basal member of Hadrosauridae or occupies a basal position in the broader Hadrosauroidea.
In 1900, Nopcsa assigned Telmatosaurus to Trachodontidae, a term that is no longer used.
Telmatosaurus transsylvanicus lived between 70 and 66 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous in what is now Europe.
The time range for Telmatosaurus is from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
At that time, the land where the fossils were found was part of the European archipelago.
The holotype fossil, consisting of a skull and lower jaws, dates to about 68 million years ago from the Maastrichtian age of the Haţeg Island.
The holotype dates to about 68 million years ago, from the Maastrichtian stage.
It is debated whether fragmentary hadrosauroid material from Spain, France, Germany, and Romania belongs to Telmatosaurus, as an identity is difficult to prove.
It is debated whether fragmentary material from Spain, France, and Germany, previously included in Orthomerus, truly belongs to Telmatosaurus, as it is difficult to prove the identity.
Some material was lost during World War II due to bombings, complicating the study of the species.
